comments.author: pcompeau

We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January.

We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

stories.title_en: Running coding agents without handing them my credentials

comments.author: blop
comments.text:
fnox (
https://fnox.jdx.dev/
) is another solution which is also fantastic for day-to-day human use in the cli. It works a bit like sops but can also chain multiple encryption providers, so for example you can use an encrypted age key with a fido2 provider (a yubikey for example) as the main provider of all the secrets on your computer.
If you run for example `fnox exec gh`, fnox will ask you to touch the yubikey to decrypt the age key and decode the github token env var for the gh cli (fnox can also cache the decoded value for a bit, like gpg agent).
You can then tell the AI agent to use `fnox exec gh` to access gh without seeing the gh token.

comments.author: h4kunamata
comments.text:
For bash and python scripting I just use keepassxc-cli.
Tokens in general is "never exposed":
keepassxc-cli show --no-password -k $KEEPASS_KEY $KEEPASS_DB "GROUP_GOES_HERE/SECRET_NAME_HERE" --attributes Password
When dealing with agents, they access the tokens the same way, it is the best balance I found between keeping things safe without adding too much complexity making my life harder.
It can save tho, have the code to also save access_token to the vault the same way, so no log/execution will ever show the secrets.
Tokens the agents use, are read-only with the minimalist access.
Never ever ever grant an agent access to any token with destructive access, unless you accepted the risks.

No big surprises here. Big outages at big firms seem to always look like this.
The electricity industry has this notion they call a black start, where they bring the grid online from zero. It's a very difficult operation because you can't start a generator straight into an offline grid otherwise it gets hit with full demand and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment. So they have to start by disconnecting all the loads and then bringing load blocks back in sequence, trying to roughly balance available generation with the size of the next block. In practice black starts are extremely rare, but they can happen after a cascading failure in which something causes some generating stations to trip, redirecting load onto the remaining stations which can't handle it causing them to trip in turn. The entire grid can collapse in just 60 seconds or so once that kind of runaway failure starts.
This kind of outage is very analogous to a black start. A few servers get into trouble - maybe they're in a crash loop or maybe their caches are cold - the load balancers shift traffic onto the remainder which then can't handle the load either and so the failure cascades. Onc

One of the things that I think makes Rust unique is that it acknowledges the possibility of human error. I think it’s also one of the most controversial too: there are certain people who get an ego hit at the insinuation that they ever could have written C code with mistakes.
Instead of hoping you remember to check for NULL, Rust forces you to make a decision on how to handle the possibility of failure. Sure, you can still pick a bad decision (unwrap) but that is at least a specific decision and you can’t forget to do it.
You can take it even further with things like the newtype pattern. If you have lots of numeric IDs (project ID, user ID, etc) you can give them distinct types so you don’t mix them up.
So Rust taught me I can program defensively against my own brain, which sometimes gets tired or lazy or distracted.

I wholeheartedly agree. I learned this lesson from learning Haskell, before I was even aware of Rust and before Rust had its 1.0 release. One of the reasons I was first excited about Rust in fact was precisely that it had a type system like that of Haskell.

comments.author: xeubie
comments.text: Rust enums conflate the tag type with the union type that uses it. These should be separate things. In the example here, you can see that Rust gives no way to represent the tag type `{Human, Cat}`. In Zig there is an enum which is a set of tags, and a union which is backed by that enum and can have fields. It is obviously better to have these as separate concepts rather than conflating them. You often want the kind without the data, and Rust gives you no way to represent it. I'm not sure why I am bothering to rant about this but it's one of my biggest annoyances with the language.

comments.author: greggman65
comments.text:
The question is why? LLMs will write this stuff without three.js just fine.
See 4 examples I posted yesterday:
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50514583
Without three.js the LLMs are more free to write whatever is appropriate for the specific project, instead of having to work around three.js:s architectural decisions when they don't match the thing being made. They further don't need any of three.s infra.
Whether or not those examples are AAA, they are proof IMO that the LLMs can do it without the libraries AND they can do it better without the shackles. Take the GTA like one above, the LLM split the city in 128 triangle chunks and culls them all on the GPU, taking inspiration from Nanite. Any feature you want they will happily recreate in 1 or 2 prompts. And no, you don't need any special knowledge. You just need to ask the LLM to optimize over a few prompts and it will figure out solutions.
I know people will jump to three.js defense because it's well loved and a great library. At the same time, so many people are acknowledging that so many libraries in general are no longer needed. See shopify getting rid of middleware because the LLM doesn't needed it:
https://shopify.engi
